FAST

Nov 6 : For the ancient Maya, the vibrant red mineral cinnabar held deep sacred meaning, representing blood, life and the soul. They used it widely as pigment in murals and temples while also employing it in ceremonies and funerary rites. What they did not know is that cinnabar is mostly mercury, which can be highly toxic. Previous research showed how mercury from cinnabar left enduring contamination at the sites of certain ancient Maya cities such as Tikal in Guatemala. A new study reveals that this contamination was more widespread than previously known and documents how mercury, after leaching into the surrounding soil and bodies of water, proved deadly for many aquatic organisms. Researchers obtained core samples from beneath lakes at two ancient Maya cities on Mexico's Yucatan peninsula — the well-studied site of Coba and the little-known site of Xcach. The samples showed a mercury spike at Coba beginning around 250 AD and lasting about 150 years around the outset of the golden age of Maya civilization, called the Classic Period. At Xcach, there was a spike from around 125 AD to 200 AD, shortly before the Classic Period, then a second spike at about the same time as the one at Coba, and a third spike from about 535 AD to 820 AD, running to around the end of the Classic Period.

The study documents mercury contamination in the Maya northern lowlands, a region with previously sparse mercury records, and reveals some of the highest recorded Maya-era mercury concentrations. Many of the great Maya cities collapsed and were abandoned at the end of the Classic Period. Varying hypotheses have been presented to explain this calamity, including climate change and warfare. The new research suggests mercury poisoning as one additional factor. "Our study shows that modern toxicology and pollution regulations were far exceeded at the most toxic levels for centuries around Coba and Xcach," said paleolimnologist Matt Waters, a professor of environmental science at Auburn University in Alabama and lead author of the study published in the journal Science Advances. "Furthermore, we measured multiple biological markers in the sediments for bacteria, algae, cyanobacteria, shelled organisms and insect midges, which all decreased or vanished in the lakes, meaning the mercury had made its way into multiple levels of the food chain," Waters said. MERCURY POISONING Mercury in people can harm the central nervous system, brain, kidneys, lungs and heart. "While we do not show this in our sediment records, this trophic movement implies that the Maya people might have been exposed to mercury via consumption of water or fish," said study co-author Savanna Wooten, a postdoctoral researcher at the Jones Center at Ichauway research facility in Georgia. "This research does little to link mercury directly to the demise of Classic-era Maya cities. But it does add one more stressor to the growing list of environmental and climatic pressures documented to have co-occurred with the Classic Period Maya," Wooten said. Coba (pronounced "koh-BAH") is estimated to have had a population of 60,000 to 90,000 people during the Classic Period. It is a well-known jungle archeological site visited by many tourists that features one of the tallest ancient pyramids in the Yucatan.  Less is known about Xcach (pronounced "SCOTCH"), a site on private land featuring multiple pyramids and structures where very little archeological work has been done. Cinnabar is a naturally occurring mercury sulfide mineral and may have been a major trade commodity in places like Coba and Xcach where it is not found in natural abundance, the researchers said. The Maya fashioned one of the great civilizations in the pre-Columbian New World, prospering in a broad area of Mexico as well as Guatemala, Belize, Honduras and El Salvador. Among other achievements, they built monumental structures, crafted great works of art, gained a sophisticated understanding of astronomy and mathematics, produced an advanced calendar and developed an intricate writing system. "Their longevity as a culture and development in science, construction and art is both extensive and elegant. Cinnabar would have been a pigment that added beauty and culture to these people," Waters said.

Source: Reuters

LONDON, Nov 6 : British media regulator Ofcom said on Friday that Snapchat had begun disabling its "Find Friends" feature by default for child users in Britain, in what it called an important step to reduce the risk of online grooming. The friend-discovery feature helps users find and add new contacts. Ofcom said the change would make it harder for strangers to contact children on the image-sharing social media platform, one it considers among the largest and most popular online services used by children in Britain. The regulator said in May that Snapchat was used by 32 per cent of children aged 8 to 12 in Britain, despite the platform's minimum age restriction of 13.

Oliver Griffiths, director of Ofcom's Online Safety Group, said the change was "long overdue" and the regulator would monitor Snapchat's rollout of the new protection this month. Snapchat had committed to make such a change in May, and told the regulator more recently that effective age checks for under 18s should be in place by the end of the year. The platform did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday. There have long been concerns about online grooming on social media. A 2025 analysis of British police data by the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children showed that 40 per cent of recorded offences involving sexual communication with a child where the platform was identified took place on Snapchat. Ofcom has pressed major tech firms to introduce stronger anti-grooming measures. It has said that online grooming can have "devastating, lifelong consequences" for children. The regulator also re-issued a warning to other tech companies failing to tackle grooming risks, saying they risked fines of up to 10 per cent of their qualifying global revenue.

Source: Reuters

Nov 6 : The English amateur cricketer who went viral for finger-clicking trickery has been handed a two-year suspension, the North Yorkshire & South Durham Cricket League said on Friday. The fielder, dubbed "Clicky Ponting" on social media in a nod to former Australia captain Ricky Ponting, was accused of tricking umpires by clicking his fingers to make the sound of a ball nicking the bat as deliveries were missed and caught by the wicketkeeper. The video footage went viral on social media and made international headlines earlier this year. A three-person disciplinary panel reviewed the footage and considered player interviews and written statements before imposing the ban. "The player concerned is suspended from all cricket under the ECB's (the England and Wales Cricket Board) jurisdiction for two years, from 30 September 2026 to 29 September 2028. This covers playing, coaching, umpiring, scoring and managing junior teams," the NYSDL said in a statement.

LISBON, Nov 6 : Portugal pledged to honour Cristiano Ronaldo on Friday as manager Jorge Jesus named his first squad since the captain's international retirement, then faced a barrage of questions about the rift that preceded the departure. The 41-year-old announced his decision on social media on Thursday, ending a Portugal career spanning 234 appearances and 146 goals. Portuguese FA president Pedro Proenca promised to celebrate Ronaldo's contribution, although there was no word on whether the forward would agree to a farewell appearance. "No tribute will ever be enough to thank him for everything he has done for Portuguese football, for Portugal," Proenca said before the squad announcement. "We will do everything we can to honour the legacy he leaves us. Everything he has done deserves to be honoured and celebrated."

Jesus selected seven new faces, including five players from the Under-21s, for November's Nations League matches against Wales and Denmark, but Ronaldo's absence dominated proceedings. The forward left Portugal's camp without permission at the end of September, ahead of a Nations League match against Denmark, and did not return. He later cited broken promises from Jesus as the reason for his departure. Jesus became visibly annoyed as journalists pressed him about the dispute, repeatedly saying he wanted to discuss his selections rather than Ronaldo. "All my decisions were made with the team in mind. As a manager, I have always defended what was best for the team. I am at peace with my decision," Jesus said, insisting there were no hard feelings. He said Ronaldo remained in his plans until Thursday's announcement. "I found out when we all did," Jesus said. "Until then, I knew nothing about it. He was playing, he was scoring goals; he was one of the players on my squad list." Jesus said he had not subsequently contacted Ronaldo. Proenca, meanwhile, said he, Jesus and everyone at the federation respected Ronaldo's decision, praising his leadership and influence on generations of Portuguese players. "The best way to honour and celebrate him is to honour his boundless ambition. To always play to win. To never be afraid of being the best in the world," he said. "Thank you for everything, captain. This is and always will be your home."

AMSTERDAM, Nov 6 : Protesters broke into the construction site of a Microsoft data centre in Amsterdam on Friday at the start of two days of rallies that are part of a growing global backlash over the rapid build-out of computing power needed for AI. Activist groups have announced actions in 16 countries on Friday and Saturday, according to the "Stop Dirty Data Centres" coalition, which is rallying environmental groups and digital rights campaigns behind calls to pause large-scale construction. In Amsterdam on Friday, more than 100 activists gathered at the construction site of a Microsoft AI data centre, marching arm in arm before breaking into the site, climbing cranes, hanging balloons and dancing while police stood by. Some carried placards with messages reading: "Screw your datacentre". "These data centres are destroying our world. It's becoming uninhabitable because of all the resources they consume. That's why we're here today," protester Sam van der Beek said.

Site owner Pure Data Centres, which plans to invest more than $1 billion and is backed by Brookfield-owned Oaktree, said it was committed to engagement with local stakeholders. "We respectfully ask those on site to leave safely and engage with us in dialogue about the development and any concerns they may have," it said. Other planned actions include a march in Dublin, a protest outside the parliament building in Warsaw, and a demonstration against a different Microsoft data centre in Denmark. Microsoft said it understood that people had strong feelings about the project and respected their right to express them peacefully but did not condone any unlawful actions. CONCERN OVER AI DRIVES STOCK MARKET ROUT Pushback is growing from Spain to India and the United States, where technology stocks fell sharply on Thursday over concern that Democratic control of Congress could mean tougher regulation curtails the AI boom. Campaigners say data centres pressure electricity and water supplies, compete with housing and other businesses for scarce resources and threaten climate goals. They also point to job losses and potential risks to personal and national security from private and big tech concentrating power. Technology companies argue that data centres are essential to meeting global demand for artificial intelligence and cloud computing and provide critical infrastructure for businesses, governments and consumers. Stop Dirty Data Centres says it is not anti-progress or calling for existing data centres to be closed but that major construction should be halted until governments establish clearer rules. Europe is divided between its ambition to catch up with the US and Asia on AI to boost productivity and to maintain what are generally more stringent controls and public protections. Speaking to Reuters on Thursday, EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said Europe needed more data centres to power AI development, though she added it needed to be done with care. "AI, of course, is a super important technology and we need to have our own capacity," Virkkunen said, pointing to investments being made in chip-making capacity, AI startups and a plan to build out gigafactories around the region. However, she added, "it's very important for citizens that they can trust that their energy bills are not skyrocketing and there's not electricity blackouts because of data centres, or they are not destroying the environment with these projects." A Google project in Finland faces a criminal probe over land clearances, Italy and Portugal are tightening environmental regulation for datacentres, and Microsoft pulled out of a UK data centre project that was hit by infrastructure delays. The Netherlands has about 200 data centres either planned, under construction or in operation.

Source: Reuters

Nov 6 : Imane Khelif is set to return to the ring for the first time since winning gold at the Paris Olympics, with the 27-year-old due to fight on December 15 in the same city where she became the Olympic champion. Algerian Khelif, who was forced out of a professional bout with Julia Igel in April due to injury, will face 21-year-old Dutch boxer Clarida Sarabia in a six-round professional fight, French media said. The bout with Sarabia, who holds an undefeated 4-0 professional record, was announced at a press conference in Paris on Friday.  Khelif has not competed at official events since winning gold in the women's welterweight division at the 2024 Olympics amid a gender dispute over her eligibility, after the International Boxing Association disqualified her from the 2023 World Championships based on sex chromosome tests.

In a video promoting the upcoming fight, Khelif said she never gave up despite the long absence from the ring. "Days became weeks, weeks became months. I waited, doubted. But deep inside, the fire never died. Behind closed doors, I kept fighting," she said in the video posted by Stair Event on Instagram. "Because this fight was never only mine. It was for everyone who dared to be, for everyone who refused to give up." World Boxing, which will oversee boxing competitions at the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles after being granted provisional recognition by the International Olympic Committee, last year announced mandatory sex testing for all boxers in its competitions. In February, Khelif said she was open to genetic testing only if administered by the IOC. When asked whether she would defend her Olympic title in 2028, Khelif told reporters: "I can't answer, because I've filed complaints against World Boxing regarding the gender tests." However, Kamel Abdesselam, who coaches Khelif alongside Nasser Lalaoui, said she would not defend the title. "She has no interest in competing in the Games again. She's already an Olympic champion," Abdesselam said.

Nov 6 : Ducati's Marc Marquez could clinch a record-equalling eighth MotoGP title in Qatar this weekend, but the reigning champion would rather not be there amid paddock unease over racing so close to a regional conflict. MotoGP officials told teams in Malaysia on Sunday they had received no information warranting a change to the Qatar Grand Prix, despite riders' concerns about the war against Iran. The race at the Lusail International Circuit, originally scheduled for April, was postponed to November 6 to 8 due to the conflict, with seven-times champion Marquez among those seeking further assurances. "Not the best place to be but, in the end, we have a contract and we are ready to race here in Qatar," said Marquez, who can equal Giacomo Agostini's haul of eight world championships in the premier class.

"I tried to arrive as late as possible and I will leave as soon as possible... You can see that some people are affected a bit more, some people a bit less. "But in the end, we must be professional." Marquez's remark contrasted with the stance taken by Aprilia, who have been vocal about wanting to race in Qatar as they look to salvage a campaign that seemed theirs to win months ago. MotoGP has said independent risk assessments show it is safe to race, while Qatar has given official assurances and guarantees that teams and riders will not be stranded if the conflict escalates. APRILIA DISMISS SAFETY DEBATE "If the organisers say it's safe, we have to go. There's not much to debate. Honestly, I don't understand all this fuss that's being made," Aprilia boss Massimo Rivola told AS. "I want to go. If you don't want to do this job, you stay home." But those assurances did not stop Yamaha from withdrawing after the Japanese manufacturer cited "company-wide travel restrictions". MotoGP said the team could face "sporting consequences" for not honouring its contract, a decision for governing body FIM, which did not respond to a Reuters request for comment. "I don't want to go. Like everybody," Pramac Racing's Jack Miller had said in Sepang. "They can attack us at any angle. Both financially and on the sporting side with our licences and also the team... Do I want to hurt the team? Not at all. But at the same time, I don't feel like pushing the horse to race." Trackhouse rider Raul Fernandez said it had been a "strange weekend" since arriving in Qatar. "The tension of there being a war going on and you being right in the thick of it... for the people working there, it's not exactly the ideal atmosphere," he said. MATCH POINT FOR MARQUEZ Marquez leads with 399 points - 44 ahead of Aprilia's Jorge Martin, who led earlier in the season, and 67 clear of Marco Bezzecchi, once a clear favourite after winning four of the first seven races. "I'm happy to be heading to Qatar. It's a track I really like," Bezzecchi said. Martin, who was declared fit on Friday after withdrawing from Malaysia with a fractured wrist, is eager to return after he saw his title hopes slowly fade. "I went back to Spain to continue the treatment I need to recover from the injury and to get to Qatar in the best shape possible. Now we'll see how the body responds," the 2024 champion said.

FAST

LEEDS, England, Nov 6 : For try lovers, England is the place to be to watch club rugby - there were 18 alone in the Northampton-Bath Prem fixture last month. The league averages 8.1 tries per game so far this season, which puts it out in front of the United Rugby Championship with 7.6 and the Top 14 in France with 7.2 as the entertainment capital of the European game. The bang for the spectator buck is undeniable, even if some of the scorelines have veered too far towards basketball for some tastes. How useful funfair rugby is as a primer for test rugby, though, we are about to find out as the Nations Championship window opens in Europe.

The concern for England coach Steve Borthwick is that - in the same way as boundary-packed T20 cricket is no sort of preparation for the five-day grind of test cricket - the domestic points bonanzas may have left his players short for the international arena. The kind of open, expressive rugby which gets the ball in the hands of the likes of England's dangerous wingers Manny Feyi-Waboso and Tommy Freeman has to be a positive in one regard. Those two in form are a handful for any defence and Freeman, in particular, who goes into Sunday's fixture against Australia with five tries in as many Prem games this season, is flying off the back of the brand of rugby English champions Northampton play. The problems come in other areas.  The breakdown contest against Australia is likely to be very different from the one in the Prem, which is heavily weighted in favour of the attacking side. Ollie Chessum, who was coached by Borthwick at Leicester when they won what was then called the Premiership in 2022, says the England coach has earmarked the breakdown for specific attention in training ahead of the game. "Steve's a very intelligent coach and he's marked that there's quite a difference in the way that is refereed in the Premiership to the way it's refereed internationally," said England forward Chessum, who is likely to wear the No. 6 shirt. "I think you saw that around that first weekend of European fixtures. Steve made the point that English teams had performed least effectively at the breakdown area.  "It's not a weakness, it's just somewhere we have to alter slightly for the way it is going to be refereed as well as trying to grow our strengths as well." BREAKDOWN CONCERNS England's eight clubs entered in the Champions Cup this season managed one win in the opening round of fixtures. The breakdown concerns are heightened this weekend because the Wallabies have access to one of the world's top poachers in Fraser McReight, who was awarded the John Eales Medal last week as Australia's player of the year. England will need to control him if they want to secure the win which will keep them in the running for the inaugural Nations Championship final at the end of the month. Turnover ball would be the magic potion Australia crave to attack off and they have the dangerous strike runners to do severe damage if they get it. England are not short on effective back rowers, including Henry Pollock, who is set for an impact role off the bench, but when the remit is different from week to week with their clubs it takes a collective recalibration when international rugby comes around. Defence is the other area Borthwick has been hammering home and, again, that is a reflection of what has been happening domestically. In some Prem games this season it has almost been an afterthought. England have defence coaches coming out of their ears with four of Borthwick's assistants - Kevin Sinfield, Joe El Abd, Byron McGuigan and Richard Wigglesworth - having dabbled in the role at one point or another. If such a set-up risks mixed messaging then Borthwick will be hoping Wigglesworth, the official incumbent, manages to put his instructions across loud and clear on Sunday.

(Editing by Christian Radnedge)

Nov 6 : Alphabet built a stake worth nearly $548 million in longtime partner Qualcomm in the third quarter, giving a boost to the chipmaker's efforts to expand into data centers as the smartphone market sees one of the worst downturns. Qualcomm shares rose 3 per cent in premarket trading. They had tumbled more than 9 per cent on Thursday after disappointing September-quarter results and a broader selloff triggered by a Democratic win in the US midterm elections. Qualcomm's chips have long powered virtually all major smartphones with Google's Android operating system. More recently, the companies collaborated on Google's new premium laptop line-up, Googlebook, that runs on processors from Qualcomm. They also struck an agreement in 2024 to build chips and software for AI adoption in the automotive industry.

WASHINGTON, Nov 6 : Democrats are planning to unleash a flood of new legislation targeting artificial intelligence systems and data-center development when they take control of the US Congress in January, lawmakers, congressional aides and advocates said.  The plans would mark a sharp shift from the Republican-led Congress, where lawmakers largely focused on promoting AI development and declined to pass legislation restricting aspects of the technology at a time when voters turned against the rapid development of data centers and their extensive power needs. Democrats plan on introducing bills aimed at shielding consumers from rising electricity costs tied to data centers, requiring independent testing of advanced AI systems and clarifying when AI companies can be held liable for harm caused by their products, they said.  Any legislation would face steep odds while President Donald Trump remains in the White House, as he has repeatedly dismissed calls to write mandatory rules for AI technology.

But Democratic lawmakers and outside advocates said control of congressional committees would give the party a platform to advance proposals, compel testimony from industry leaders and build support for action if AI systems cause real-world harm. Representative Greg Casar, a Texas Democrat and chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, already said this week that AI executives should be called to testify under oath. Federal government restrictions on AI development could hurt the industry's profits if they slow the release of new models or prompt the companies to change how their AI tools perform to address concerns that their products are harming people. Technology shares sold off dramatically on Thursday on growing concerns that a new Congress will slow AI development, but also on fears that the massive capital expense on building out AI will not yield sufficient returns. MULTIPLE BILLS LIKELY Senator Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat who is expected to become majority leader, said on Thursday at an event in Washington that protecting consumers from higher energy costs linked to the rapid expansion of data centers would be among his priorities next year.  Representative Lori Trahan of Massachusetts, one of the Democratic Party's leading voices on AI policy, plans to push legislation requiring independent experts to evaluate leading AI models against safety standards, said Francis Grubar, her deputy chief of staff. Trahan will also pursue legislation clarifying that companies can be held responsible when AI systems act in harmful ways, he said. Representative Zoe Lofgren, a Democrat from California who is seeking to chair the House Science Committee, said Democrats would focus on developing "responsible regulations for AI while also fostering innovation." Abdul El-Sayed, a Michigan Democrat who won a Senate seat on Tuesday, called during his campaign for an independent agency to oversee AI regulation with the power to police tech companies developing the technology.  Public concern about AI is already high. Most US voters think Trump's administration and Congress are not taking the risks of AI seriously enough and want the government to write new regulations for the technology, according to a Reuters poll published in October. A crisis could build enough support to overcome presidential opposition to AI regulation, said Ed Mills, who manages policy research at Raymond James. "The probability of legislation is much higher than people anticipate," he said.  Congress can override a presidential veto with the backing of two-thirds of lawmakers in both chambers. Democrats could also try to insert AI regulation into routine bills that must pass Congress each year, Mills said. Democrats also plan to use their new authority to intensify scrutiny of the industry's most powerful companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic. Lofgren and other Democratic House committee leaders in October asked OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Alphabet's Google and SpaceX to detail their security practices and report instances of their AI tools taking actions that their designers did not intend.
